section.title: The Ministry of the Apostles
section.sectionRationale: Having called the leaders mere servants and farmers and builders, Paul now defines what an apostle truly is: a servant of Christ and a steward of God's mysteries, answerable to the Lord rather than to any human court. He then unmasks the Corinthians' inflated self-image by contrasting their supposed wealth and reign with the apostles' suffering, portraying the apostles as a spectacle appointed for death, the refuse of the world. Yet he writes as a father to beloved children, urging them to imitate him, and warns that the kingdom of God is not talk but power.
section.thesis: Apostles are servants of Christ and stewards of God's mysteries, judged not by human verdicts but by the Lord who will expose every heart; and true apostolic ministry looks not like the Corinthians' proud self-sufficiency but like a suffering spectacle, so that as their father in the gospel Paul calls them to imitate his cruciform life and to reckon with a kingdom that is power, not mere talk.
section.frameNote: Three movements: apostles as servants and stewards awaiting the Lord's judgment; the suffering spectacle of the apostles set against the Corinthians' inflated pride; and Paul the father warning and appealing to his beloved children, for the kingdom is power not talk.

units.label: Servants and stewards, judged by the Lord
units.note: faithfulness required, the Lord alone judges

verses.text: So then, men ought to regard us as servants of Christ and {{oikonomos|stewards}} of the {{mysterion|mysteries}} of God.
Now it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.
I care very little, however, if I am judged by you or by any human court. In fact, I do not even judge myself.
My conscience is clear, but that does not vindicate me. It is the Lord who judges me.

Therefore judge nothing before the appointed time; wait until the Lord comes. He will bring to light what is hidden in darkness and will expose the motives of men’s hearts. At that time each will receive his praise from God.

units.label: The suffering spectacle of the apostles
units.note: what do you have that you did not receive

verses.text: Brothers, I have applied these things to myself and Apollos for your benefit, so that you may learn from us not to go beyond what is written. Then you will not take pride in one man over another.
For who makes you so superior? What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you did not?
Already you have all you want. Already you have become rich. Without us, you have become kings. How I wish you really were kings, so that we might be kings with you!

For it seems to me that God has displayed us apostles at the end of the procession, like prisoners appointed for death. We have become a {{theatron|spectacle}} to the whole world, to angels as well as to men.
We are fools for Christ, but you are wise in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You are honored, but we are dishonored.
To this very hour we are hungry and thirsty, we are poorly clothed, we are brutally treated, we are homeless.
We work hard with our own hands. When we are vilified, we bless; when we are persecuted, we endure it;
when we are slandered, we answer gently. Up to this moment we have become the scum of the earth, the refuse of the world.

units.label: A father's warning and appeal
units.note: imitate me, for the kingdom is power not talk

verses.text: I am not writing this to shame you, but to warn you as my beloved children.
Even if you have ten thousand guardians in Christ, you do not have many fathers; for in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel.
Therefore I urge you to imitate me.
That is why I have sent you Timothy, my beloved and faithful child in the Lord. He will remind you of my way of life in Christ Jesus, which is exactly what I teach everywhere in every church.
Some of you have become arrogant, as if I were not coming to you.
But I will come to you shortly, if the Lord is willing, and then I will find out not only what these arrogant people are saying, but what power they have.
For the {{basileia|kingdom}} of God is not a matter of talk but of power.
Which do you prefer? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and with a gentle spirit?

oikonomos.gloss: A household steward or manager, a trusted servant put in charge of a master's estate and goods. An oikonomos owns nothing but administers what belongs to another and answers to the master alone. Paul casts the apostles as stewards of God's household, entrusted with the gospel, whose one requirement is faithfulness, not popularity.

mysterion.gloss: A mystery, a truth once hidden and now revealed by God. In Paul it is not a secret to be earned but the open secret of the gospel, above all Christ crucified and the salvation of the nations. The apostles are stewards of these mysteries, dispensing to the church what God has unveiled in Christ.

theatron.gloss: A theatre, and by extension the spectacle put on display before it. Paul pictures the apostles as condemned prisoners paraded at the end of a Roman triumph, a public show for the whole world, angels and men alike. Far from the honour the Corinthians craved, apostleship means becoming a spectacle of shame for Christ's sake.

basileia.gloss: Kingdom, the reign and rule of God breaking into the world. Paul says the kingdom is not a matter of talk but of power, contrasting the Corinthians' impressive words with the Spirit's transforming power. The kingdom advances not through eloquence and status but through the power of God at work in servants who suffer for Christ.

basic.context: The Corinthians were sizing up their leaders like celebrities and passing verdicts on them. Paul says: think of us rightly, as servants of Christ and stewards entrusted with God's message. The only question that matters is whether a steward is faithful, and the only judge who matters is the Lord, who will one day expose every hidden thing. Then Paul punctures their pride. They imagine they are rich and reigning like kings, while the real apostles are hungry, homeless, beaten, treated like the world's garbage, a public spectacle for Christ. Yet Paul writes as their father in the gospel, warning them in love and reminding them that God's kingdom runs on power, not talk.
basic.hermeneutics: Paul mixes sharp irony, verse 8, with tender appeal, verse 14, to correct without crushing. He uses himself and Apollos as living illustrations of not going beyond what is written. The suffering catalogue is not self-pity but a portrait of cruciform ministry that exposes the emptiness of the Corinthians' triumphalism.
basic.originalLanguages: Apostles are oikonomoi, household stewards, who own nothing and answer to the master alone, entrusted with the mysterion, the open secret of the gospel now revealed in Christ. Paul pictures them as a theatron, a spectacle, condemned prisoners paraded at the end of a triumph for all to jeer. And he ends with basileia: the kingdom of God is not talk but power.
basic.typology: The suffering apostle who blesses when cursed and endures when persecuted embodies the pattern of Christ, who was despised and rejected yet reigns. The steward entrusted with his master's goods echoes the servants in Jesus' parables who must be found faithful when the master returns.
basic.christ: The whole portrait of apostleship is cross-shaped, tracing the path of Christ Himself: made a spectacle, dishonoured, treated as the refuse of the world, yet faithful. Paul became the Corinthians' father through the gospel, that is, through Christ crucified and risen. And the coming of the Lord is the appointed time when hidden things are brought to light, so all present verdicts wait for His.
basic.god: God is the master who entrusts His mysteries to stewards and requires faithfulness. He is the righteous judge who sees what is hidden in darkness, exposes the motives of the heart, and gives each his due praise. And His kingdom comes not by human eloquence but by His own power, so that boasting is silenced and glory goes to Him.
basic.crossReferences: In Luke 12 the faithful and wise steward is set over the household to give food at the proper time. Second Corinthians 4 speaks of treasure in jars of clay so the power belongs to God. Colossians 1 calls the gospel the mystery now revealed. Philippians 3 urges believers to imitate Paul as he follows Christ.
basic.oneStory: God's kingdom advances through servants who carry the gospel at great cost, following the crucified and risen Lord. The Corinthians wanted a kingdom of comfort and status now; Paul points them to the pattern of the cross, where suffering service precedes glory. The story runs from the humble ministry of Christ, through the suffering of His apostles, to the day the Lord comes and brings every hidden thing to light.

context.literary:
Chapter 4 completes the first major section of the letter, the long treatment of the Corinthian factions that began at 1:10. Paul has argued from the cross, from the Spirit, and from the picture of God's field and building. Now he turns to the practical question that sits underneath all of it: how should a church regard its leaders, and how should leaders regard themselves? The answer comes in four movements. Verses 1 to 5 define the apostle as a steward under judgment. Verses 6 to 13 expose the Corinthians' pride by comparing their lives with the apostles' lives. Verses 14 to 17 shift into the voice of a father. Verses 18 to 21 close with a warning about a coming visit.

The central block, verses 8 to 13, is one of the most carefully built passages in the letter. It begins with three short biting sentences in the past tense, 'Already you have all you want. Already you have become rich. Without us, you have become kings,' verse 8, and then breaks into a wish and a picture, the apostles at the end of the procession, verse 9. Verse 10 sets three pairs side by side, fools and wise, weak and strong, honoured and dishonoured. Verses 11 to 13 are a list of hardships, followed by the three paired responses, 'we bless,' 'we endure,' 'we answer gently.' Each response is the opposite of the natural reaction.

The tone shifts sharply at verse 14. Paul has been using irony as a scalpel, and he stops to say plainly that he did not write to shame them. He then names the relationship that explains the severity: 'my beloved children,' verse 14, and 'I became your father,' verse 15. The whole passage ends with a choice put as a question, the rod or love and a gentle spirit, verse 21.

The two uses of 'arrogant' in verses 18 and 19 and the earlier 'take pride' in verse 6 are the same verb in Greek. The bracket tells us what the passage is about. Pride, not doctrine, is the target.
context.historical:
Corinth was a city obsessed with honour. It had been refounded as a colony of Roman settlers, and many of its people were traders and freedmen who had made their own way, so display counted for more than family. Wealth and display were the road to status, and a person's standing was constantly measured. In that setting, the apostle's lot as Paul describes it, hunger, homelessness, manual labour and beatings, was a social disgrace. Hard physical work with one's own hands, verse 12, was despised by the educated classes. Paul worked as a tentmaker, Acts 18:3, and refused to be a fee taking teacher at Corinth, as he explains in chapter 9.

The image in verse 9 is of a Roman triumph, a public parade for a victorious general. At the very end of the procession came the captives, and some of them were destined to be put to death. The crowds lined the road to watch. Paul says that this is the place God has given to the apostles, last in line, condemned, a 'spectacle,' theatron, which is the word for a theatre and for what is shown in it. He adds 'to angels as well as to men,' so the show is cosmic. In 2 Corinthians 2:14 he uses the picture again from the other side, where God leads him in triumphal procession.

The title 'steward' also had a precise social meaning. A steward, oikonomos, was usually a slave or freedman who managed his master's household. He owned nothing and answered to the owner. Paul's friend Erastus, who sent greetings from Corinth, held the office of 'city treasurer,' Romans 16:23, which uses the same word. The Corinthians knew what a steward's trust involved, and what it meant to be examined at the end.

The guardians of verse 15 were a familiar figure in Greek households. A paidagogos was a trusted slave who led a child to school and supervised his conduct. He was important, but he was not the father. The contrast speaks to the Corinthians' many teachers: they could have many tutors, but only one man had brought them to birth by the gospel.
context.canonical:
The language of stewardship is at home in the Old Testament and in Jesus' teaching. Joseph's steward ran his household, Genesis 43:19, and the prophets speak of those entrusted with a master's goods. In the parables of Jesus, the steward who is faithful and wise is set over the household and is given his master's food to distribute at the proper time, Luke 12:42, and the unfaithful steward is called to account, Luke 16:1-2. Paul's statement that stewards must be found faithful draws on the same pattern. Titus 1:7 applies it to overseers: 'As God's steward, an overseer must be above reproach.'

The idea that human verdicts do not settle a person's standing recalls the Psalms and the prophets. 'Man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart,' 1 Samuel 16:7. Paul's statement that the Lord will 'expose the motives of men's hearts' belongs to that tradition, and to Romans 2:16 and Revelation 2:23. His remark that even a clear conscience does not vindicate him matches Psalm 19:12, where the psalmist asks to be cleansed from hidden faults.

The suffering of the apostles has its closest Old Testament match in the experience of the prophets. Jesus told His disciples that the prophets who came before them were persecuted in the same way, Matthew 5:12, and the book of Acts shows the apostles being beaten and rejoicing, Acts 5:40-41. Paul's long lists of hardships appear again in 2 Corinthians 4:8-12, 6:4-10 and 11:23-29. The command to respond to cursing with blessing comes from Jesus, Luke 6:28, and Paul repeats it in Romans 12:14.

The ideal of the father who warns his children has a long history. In the book of Proverbs the wise father instructs his son, and in 1 Thessalonians 2:11 Paul says he treated each of them 'as a father treats his own children.' The close of the chapter returns to the kingdom, a theme that runs from the Psalms to the preaching of Jesus. When Paul says that the kingdom is not talk but power, he is echoing the way Jesus announced it, with deeds as well as words, Matthew 12:28.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul is correcting a church that has begun to treat its leaders like celebrities and itself like a court. He wants them to see three things. First, that leaders are accountable to the Lord and not to a vote. This frees Paul from their verdicts, and he says so without bitterness, but it also binds the Corinthians, who must 'judge nothing before the appointed time,' verse 5. Second, that what they have is a gift. The question in verse 7, 'What do you have that you did not receive?' strips away the ground for any boasting about teachers, gifts or knowledge.

Third, he wants them to feel the contrast between their comfort and the life of those who brought them the gospel. The sentences about being kings are meant to sting, and Paul says outright that he is not writing to shame them, verse 14. The sarcasm is the last thing a wounded father would use to make a child look up. Behind it is a wish: 'How I wish you really were kings, so that we might be kings with you!' verse 8. He does not want to take their blessings away; he wants them to see what the blessings cost.

The first hearers were to leave with a changed picture of what leadership is. A church leader is not a patron or an entertainer but a steward and a father. And the church itself should not prize impressive talk but power, verse 20.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of the passage describes. The list of hardships in verses 11 to 13 reports what the apostles actually suffered. It is not a rule that every believer, or every minister, must be hungry, homeless and beaten, and Paul himself wishes the Corinthians well. The prescriptive part is the attitude and the response: to be found faithful, to refuse boasting, to bless when cursed and to answer slander gently.

Verse 16, 'I urge you to imitate me,' is a direct appeal, but its scope is set by verse 17, where Paul says that Timothy will remind them of his 'way of life in Christ Jesus,' and by 11:1, 'You are to imitate me, just as I imitate Christ.' The pattern to follow is Paul's way of following Christ: his humility, his service and his willingness to suffer. It is not a claim that every aspect of his life is a model.

Verse 5, 'judge nothing before the appointed time,' is also not a ban on all assessment in the church. In chapter 5 Paul will rebuke the church for failing to judge a flagrant case. The command is aimed at the hasty ranking of persons and at pronouncing on hidden motives, which belong to the Lord. Public conduct is different, and Paul says elsewhere that leaders must be tested, 1 Timothy 3:10.

debates.question: What is the meaning of 'not to go beyond what is written' in verse 6?

views.label: Stay within Scripture
views.case: The phrase 'what is written' is the perfect form of the verb that Paul uses for Old Testament quotations elsewhere in this very argument, 1:19, 1:31, 2:9 and 3:19. On this view he is pointing back to those verses, which demolish human boasting, and telling the Corinthians to let Scripture, not Corinthian fashion, set their estimate of teachers.

views.label: A familiar saying
views.case: The Greek of the phrase is abrupt, with no verb, which suggests a proverb or slogan that the Corinthians knew. On this reading Paul quotes a short rule, such as a motto about keeping to the rules, and uses it to curb their pride.

views.label: A later note that crept into the text
views.case: A few scholars have suggested that the phrase began as a marginal note and was copied into the text. Most do not accept this, since there is no manuscript evidence for omitting it.

debates.bearing: The first view is the most widely held because it fits Paul's usage in the same section. All three readings agree on the pastoral aim, that human leaders must not be exalted above what God has said about them.

debates.question: How does 'judge nothing before the appointed time' fit with Paul's demand for judgment in chapter 5?

views.label: Different objects of judgment
views.case: In 4:5 the question is the hidden motive and final worth of a servant, which only the Lord knows. In 5:12 the question is open, public conduct inside the church. Paul forbids the first and commands the second.

views.label: Different kinds of verdict
views.case: The judgment of 4:5 is a final verdict on a person's standing and reward. The judgment of chapter 5 is a provisional act of church discipline that protects the community and aims at restoration.

debates.bearing: Both views draw the same line: the church may and must act on what is public and clear, but it may not take the Lord's place in pronouncing on the heart. The next chapter shows Paul doing exactly that.

debates.question: How far is the church to imitate Paul in verse 16?

views.label: His pattern of cruciform life
views.case: The following verse describes what Paul wants them to remember, his 'way of life in Christ Jesus.' This is about Paul's humility, suffering and service, which follow Christ. 11:1 makes the limit explicit.

views.label: His authority as a founder
views.case: Some readers stress the father and children image and take the imitation to include submission to Paul's apostolic leadership. In the next verses he threatens to come with a rod.

debates.bearing: The two readings do not clash. A child imitates a father, and the father here directs his children to Christ. But the imitation is of Christlikeness and not of the personal details of Paul's life.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 offers two titles. 'Servants' is hyperetai, from a word that originally meant an under-rower, one who pulls an oar beneath the captain's direction. It is used for attendants who carry out orders, as in Luke 1:2 for those who served the word and in Acts 26:16 where Paul is made a servant and witness. 'Stewards' is oikonomoi, the managers of a household's goods. The two words are different pictures. The first stresses obedience to a commander and the second stresses trust for another's property. Together they make leaders answerable twice over.

In verse 3 the phrase 'any human court' is literally 'a human day,' a deliberate contrast with the Day of the Lord in 3:13 and the 'appointed time' of verse 5. A human day is a trial convened by men. The verb for 'judge,' anakrino, is the same one that appears in 2:14 and 2:15 for spiritual discernment. It means to sift and examine, and it is a good word for what a Corinthian jury might do to a teacher, which Paul refuses to accept as final.

In verse 4 Paul writes that his conscience is clear, which in Greek is 'I know nothing against myself.' He then adds that 'that does not vindicate me.' The verb is dikaioo, to justify, the great word of Romans and Galatians. So even in a passage about ministry, Paul uses the vocabulary of justification: a clean conscience does not make a person righteous before God, only the Lord's verdict does.

The 'applied' of verse 6 is metaschematizo, which means to change the form of something and to transfer it. It is used in 2 Corinthians 11:13-15 of false apostles who disguise themselves. Here it is positive. Paul has dressed up the argument in the names of himself and Apollos, a rhetorical device, which many readers think lets him speak of the Corinthians' favourites without naming the real leaders of the factions. The verb 'take pride' in verse 6 and 'arrogant' in verses 18 and 19 are the same word, physioo, to puff up. Most of its New Testament uses are in this letter, and it recurs at 5:2, 8:1 and 13:4.

Verse 7 asks 'who makes you so superior?' The verb diakrino means to distinguish or to set apart. The question is who has set the Corinthians apart from everyone else, and the answer is that someone gave them what they have. In verse 8 'become kings' is an aorist, ebasileusate, which sounds as if they have already begun to reign. It is the language of an over-realised kingdom, and Paul's reply, 'I wish you really did reign,' marks the difference between the already and the not yet.

In verse 9 the 'prisoners appointed for death' is epithanatioi, men condemned to die, and 'spectacle' is theatron. In verse 13 the 'scum' and 'refuse' are two words for what is scraped away in cleaning, the dirt and the sweepings. They are among the strongest terms of contempt Paul uses anywhere.

In verse 14 the verb 'warn' is noutheteo, to admonish and correct with the aim of changing the mind, the word behind the noun used in Ephesians 6:4 for the discipline of the Lord. And in verse 21 'a gentle spirit' is literally a spirit of gentleness, the same expression as Galatians 6:1, where those who are spiritual are told to restore a person caught in a trespass 'with a spirit of gentleness.'

typology.type: The steward faithful until the master returns
typology.fulfillment: Joseph's chief steward in Genesis 43:19 is a household manager who answers to his master. In Jesus' parables the steward is set over the household and given food to distribute, Luke 12:42, and the master returns to find him at work. Paul's apostle is such a steward, entrusted with the 'mysteries of God,' and the Lord's coming in verse 5 is the master's return. The escalation is that the household is the church, the goods are the gospel and the master is Christ Himself. The type falls short in that earthly masters can be harsh and arbitrary, while this Master's verdict brings praise to each servant, verse 5.

typology.type: The apostles in the triumphal procession
typology.fulfillment: The Roman triumph was a parade of victory with defeated captives at the end. Paul takes the picture and puts the apostles in the captive's place, appointed for death, a spectacle to the world. The correspondence is with the cross itself, where the Lord of glory was made a public spectacle. The escalation is that for Paul the apostles' humiliation shows Christ's victory, since in 2 Corinthians 2:14 God leads them in triumphal procession. The pattern is not a literal type but a way in which the shape of Christ's death is repeated in His servants, and it falls short in that only Christ's death is redemptive.

typology.type: The suffering prophets and the suffering Servant
typology.fulfillment: The prophets of Israel were mocked, beaten and killed, as Jesus says in Matthew 5:12 and 23:37. The Servant of Isaiah 53 is 'despised and rejected by men,' Isaiah 53:3. The apostles who bless when cursed, endure persecution and answer slander gently stand in this line. The correspondence is in the pattern of faithful speech met with hostility. The escalation is that the apostles bear the message of the One who has already suffered and risen, so their suffering is not defeat. It falls short as a type of atonement, since the Servant's suffering is the only one that bears sin.

Paul says 'in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel,' verse 15. The pattern is the way that God Himself is Father to His people, and in the Old Testament the prophets and teachers are sometimes called fathers, as Elisha calls Elijah in 2 Kings 2:12. The apostle's fatherhood is a share in the Father's giving of life through Christ. The escalation is that his fathering is not biological but by the gospel, the means by which the Spirit gives new birth, John 3:5-8. It falls short in that no human is the source of life, as Paul reminded them in 3:7.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ in the shape of ministry. Paul describes the apostles as appointed for death, a spectacle, fools, weak, dishonoured, hungry, homeless, the refuse of the world. This is a portrait of the life of Christ passed on to His servants. The Lord of glory was made a spectacle on the cross. He was called a fool, a deceiver and a madman. He had nowhere to lay His head, Luke 9:58. He blessed those who cursed Him, and on the cross He prayed for those who crucified Him. When Paul says 'when we are vilified, we bless,' he is describing the apostles taking on the pattern of their Master, as 1 Peter 2:23 says of Jesus, 'When they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate.'

The Corinthians' triumphalism is also a denial of the cross. They think they have already come into the kingdom's glory. Paul says that in the age before the Lord's return the road to glory is the road of the cross. This is the pattern in Romans 8:17, where believers are 'heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ,' if indeed 'we suffer with Him, so that we may also be glorified with Him.' To want glory without the cross is to want a different Christ.

The judgment of the Lord is the judgment of Christ. 'It is the Lord who judges me,' verse 4, and 'wait until the Lord comes,' verse 5. Paul usually means Jesus by 'the Lord,' and 2 Corinthians 5:10 says plainly that we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ. This is a source of both terror and comfort. Paul can ignore the verdict of the Corinthian court, and even his own, because he knows the one who will judge. The Judge is also the One who died for him. This is the gospel's answer to the anxious conscience: the final verdict belongs to the Lord who gave Himself.

Paul's fatherhood points to Christ too. He became their father 'in Christ Jesus' and 'through the gospel,' so the life he gave them was Christ's life. The apostle does not make disciples for himself. The gentle and the stern sides of his appeal, the rod or love, follow the character of Christ, who was gentle and humble in heart, Matthew 11:29, and who also overturned the tables in the temple.

Finally, the kingdom 'is not a matter of talk but of power,' verse 20, and the power is the power of the cross and resurrection, 1:18. Christ crucified is the power of God, and where His kingdom comes it is seen in changed lives, not in fine speeches. The Corinthians will have a chance to see the evidence when Paul arrives.
study.god:
Every line of the passage assumes that God owns what He hands out. What the apostles hold is on loan, and so is everything the Corinthians hold. 'What do you have that you did not receive?' verse 7. The doctrine behind that question is that God is the giver of every good thing, and that human boasting is a kind of theft, taking credit for what was freely given.

God is also the judge who sees the hidden. Verse 5 says the Lord 'will bring to light what is hidden in darkness and will expose the motives of men's hearts.' No human court can reach so far. God alone knows motives, as Jeremiah 17:10 says, 'I, the LORD, search the heart; I examine the mind.' This is a warning, because nothing is hidden, and it is also a relief, because misjudged people will be known as they are. Paul's confidence is not in his own record but in the Lord's judgment, which is true.

God is generous in His judgment. 'At that time each will receive his praise from God,' verse 5. The word is praise, not only verdict. The God who exposes motives also commends what is good. The faithful steward does not end in dread but in the master's approval, as in Matthew 25:21, 'Well done, good and faithful servant.' This reveals a God who delights in His servants, even imperfect ones.

God's way of working is by weakness. He has 'displayed us apostles at the end of the procession,' verse 9. Paul sees his sufferings as God's own placing, not as a failure of divine care. God chooses to display His power through those who look like the world's rubbish, so that the power may be seen to be His, 2 Corinthians 4:7. The kingdom comes in power, but it is the power of a crucified Lord, and God is not embarrassed by that.

God is also a father. Paul's own fatherhood is a shadow of His, and the way Paul warns his 'beloved children' is a picture of how God deals with His. God disciplines in love, Hebrews 12:6, and He is willing to come with a rod, if it is necessary, and prefers to come in love. The question of verse 21 reflects God's own character.

For worship, this means that the church should be content to leave judgment to the Lord, to honour its leaders as stewards and not as stars, and to boast in no one but Him. It should look for His power, not for talk, and it should be willing to hear the warning of a father.

crossReferences.note: 'Who then is the faithful and wise manager, whom the master puts in charge of his servants to give them their portion at the proper time?' Jesus' question is the background to Paul's 'it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.' The steward is rewarded when the master finds him at his work.

Erastus, 'the city treasurer,' sends greetings from Corinth. Paul uses the same Greek word for a city officer that he uses for the apostles as 'stewards.' The Corinthians knew from a member of their own congregation what it meant to be entrusted with another's money and to account for it.

'Man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart.' Samuel is told this when he is tempted to judge Jesse's eldest son by his appearance and height. The text lies behind Paul's refusal to be judged by human standards and his appeal to the one who sees motives.

'I, the LORD, search the heart; I examine the mind to reward a man according to his way, by what his deeds deserve.' The same God who is said to search hearts in the Old Testament is the one who will 'expose the motives of men's hearts' in 1 Corinthians 4:5, and the verse also speaks of reward, as Paul does.

Paul lists afflictions, being struck down but not destroyed, and says he carries around in his body the death of Jesus. It is the same picture as 1 Corinthians 4:9-13, with the reason given: so that the life of Jesus may also be shown in the very body that is wearing out.

'But thanks be to God, who always leads us triumphantly as captives in Christ.' It uses the same picture as 1 Corinthians 4:9, the Roman victory parade, but sees it from the angle of God's victory. The apostles in the procession are visible proof that the gospel advances through those who seem defeated.

'Join one another in following my example, brothers, and carefully observe those who walk according to the pattern we set for you.' The same call to imitation as 1 Corinthians 4:16, in a letter that shows what the pattern is, the loss of all things for the sake of Christ, Philippians 3:7-8.

Paul describes himself as gentle like a nursing mother and says he treated each of them 'as a father treats his own children.' The two pictures show the balance in 1 Corinthians 4:14-21, where he is both tender and ready to be stern. It shows that fatherhood was Paul's habitual way of seeing his ministry.

Paul stayed in Corinth and worked with Aquila and Priscilla because they were tentmakers like him. This is the background to 'we work hard with our own hands,' verse 12. The Corinthians had watched him labour at a trade, a thing their culture despised in a teacher.

'Bless those who curse you, pray for those who mistreat you.' Paul's report that 'when we are vilified, we bless' shows an apostle living out the teaching of Jesus. The words of the Lord and the conduct of His servant are the same, which is part of why Paul can ask for imitation.

'Well done, good and faithful servant! You have been faithful with a few things; I will put you in charge of many things.' It is the praise from God that Paul expects at the Lord's coming, 4:5. The faithful steward's reward is the master's own delight.

'You who are spiritual should restore him with a spirit of gentleness.' The same phrase appears in 1 Corinthians 4:21, 'in love and with a gentle spirit.' Paul sees correction as aimed at restoration, and the manner of correction is part of the message.

study.oneStory:
From the garden onward the human story is a story about who will be in charge. The serpent promised that the woman and the man would be like God, Genesis 3:5, and the result was a world of rivals, Cain and Abel, Babel's tower, kings who were gods in their own eyes. Israel's own history repeats the pattern. The people asked for a king like the other nations, 1 Samuel 8:5, and the kings often used their power for themselves. The prophets called for shepherds who would care for the flock instead of feeding themselves, Ezekiel 34:1-10.

Into this world God sends His own Son in the form of a servant. Jesus, who was in the form of God, took the form of a slave and was obedient to death, Philippians 2:6-8. He tells His disciples that the rulers of the nations lord it over them, but that it must not be so among them. The greatest must become the servant, Mark 10:42-45. The passage in 1 Corinthians 4 is that teaching applied to a church that had forgotten it. The apostles are stewards and fathers, not rulers, and their lives show the pattern of the king who died for His people.

The passage also tells where the story is going. The Corinthians were living as if the kingdom had already come in full. Paul says that it has begun, and that its power is real, verse 20, but that the age of glory has not yet arrived. The apostles are still at the end of the procession. That holds the tension between the 'already' and the 'not yet' that marks the whole New Testament. The Lord will come, hidden things will come to light, and each servant will receive praise from God, verse 5.

The final form of the story is the one that Paul wished for sarcastically in verse 8: 'How I wish you really were kings, so that we might be kings with you!' In the new creation this wish comes true without irony. Revelation 5:10 says that the Lamb has made His people 'a kingdom and priests to serve our God, and they will reign upon the earth,' and 2 Timothy 2:12 says 'if we endure, we will also reign with Him.' The road there is the road of the cross. The apostles walked it first, and the church follows, until the day when the Lord who was made a spectacle is seen by all.

quiz.q: How does Paul say the apostles should be regarded?

options.text: As servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God.
options.note: Verse 1 defines them as servants and stewards entrusted with God's gospel.

options.text: As gifted orators who have earned a loyal following.
options.note: This is the Corinthian view Paul is correcting, not his definition.

options.text: As independent authorities answerable to no one.
options.note: Stewards answer to the master; Paul says the Lord judges him.

options.text: As the ultimate judges of the church's disputes.
options.note: Paul defers judgment to the Lord, not to the apostles or the church.

quiz.q: Whose judgment ultimately matters for Paul's ministry?

options.text: The Lord's, who will expose hidden motives at the appointed time.
options.note: Verses 4 and 5 make the Lord the true judge who reveals the heart.

options.text: His own clear conscience.
options.note: Paul says his conscience is clear, but that does not vindicate him.

options.text: The verdict of the Corinthian church.
options.note: He cares very little for their court or any human court.

options.text: The opinion of the wider culture in Corinth.
options.note: Human courts and cultural approval are exactly what he sets aside.

quiz.q: What is the point of the question, 'What do you have that you did not receive?'

options.text: Everything they have is a gift, so boasting is absurd.
options.note: Verse 7 undercuts pride by tracing every good to God's gift.

options.text: They should be grateful but may still take some credit.
options.note: Paul allows no credit; the whole point is that all is received.

options.text: They had actually earned their spiritual gifts.
options.note: The rhetorical question denies this outright.

options.text: God gives more to those who boast confidently.
options.note: Boasting is precisely what Paul is dismantling.

quiz.q: How does Paul describe the apostles' actual experience?

options.text: A spectacle appointed for death, hungry, homeless, the refuse of the world.
options.note: Verses 9 to 13 portray apostleship as cruciform suffering.

options.text: Comfortable and honoured, reigning as kings already.
options.note: That is the Corinthians' illusion, which Paul contrasts with reality.

options.text: Free from any hardship because of their calling.
options.note: The catalogue lists exactly the opposite: real and constant hardship.

options.text: Admired by all the world for their eloquence.
options.note: They are treated as fools and scum, not admired.

quiz.q: In what spirit does Paul write and appeal to the Corinthians?

options.text: As a father warning beloved children and urging them to imitate him.
options.note: Verses 14 and 15 cast Paul as their father through the gospel.

options.text: As a stranger issuing cold commands.
options.note: He writes with fatherly love, not detached authority.

options.text: Only to shame them for their failures.
options.note: He explicitly says he does not write to shame but to warn.

options.text: To hand over his authority to the arrogant among them.
options.note: He warns the arrogant that he will test their power, not yield to them.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean that the kingdom of God is not talk but power?

options.text: God's reign shows itself in real transforming power, not impressive words.
options.note: Verse 20 contrasts empty talk with the Spirit's power.

options.text: Words never matter in the Christian life at all.
options.note: Words matter, but they must be backed by God's power, not replace it.

options.text: The kingdom is mainly about political force.
options.note: The power in view is God's transforming work, not political might.

options.text: Eloquent speech alone proves someone belongs to the kingdom.
options.note: Paul says the opposite: talk without power proves nothing.

questions: Paul lived to be found faithful before the Lord rather than approved by people. Whose verdict are you most tempted to live for, and how would living for the Lord's change things?
Everything you have is a gift you received. Where does that truth quietly undo a boast or comparison you have been carrying?
The apostles blessed when cursed and endured when persecuted. How might that cruciform pattern reshape the way you respond to mistreatment this week?
Paul was willing to be counted a fool and the world's refuse for Christ. Where does following Jesus cost you status, and are you willing to pay it?
The kingdom of God is power, not talk. Where in your life is there impressive talk that needs to become real, Spirit-worked power?
Paul calls the Corinthians to imitate him as he imitates Christ. Whose life would you point a younger believer to imitate, and is your own life worth imitating in that way?

translationNotes.note: Not to go beyond what is written likely calls the Corinthians to keep their estimate of leaders under Scripture; some take it as a known proverb, but either way it curbs pride in one man over another.

Displayed us at the end of the procession pictures condemned prisoners paraded last in a Roman triumph, appointed for death; the word for spectacle is theatron, the show put on before a watching world.
Guardians renders a word for the household slave who escorted and disciplined a child; Paul contrasts many such guardians with the one father who gave them life through the gospel.
